title: Less advice

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's song for Saul and Jonathan, and six honest lines of your own. Your line was my lament. Did you keep them somewhere safe? Day seven hundred forty-one.

My mom's back in the hospital. Six words, and before they've finished landing, the suggestions arrive. Have you tried a second opinion? You need to take a week off. My cousin had the same thing, and she did this. Every one of them kind. Hardly any of them asked for. The person who said those six words is still standing there, now holding a small pile of homework on top of the worry. Today is about the urge to fix, and what happens when it waits.
screen: `MY MOM'S BACK IN THE HOSPITAL.` → `THE SUGGESTIONS ARRIVE.` → `KIND, AND NOT ASKED FOR.`

segments.voice: First, Job, briefly. After chapter upon chapter of his friends' explanations, Job's verdict on all that talk, in the King James Bible, is short: "miserable comforters are ye all." Every answer they gave was meant to help. None of it comforted him. Second, James. The letter of James puts the order of things in one line: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak." Notice the order. Hearing comes first, and fast. Speaking comes second, and slowly. A ready answer is the fast part, and the letter asks for it to be the slow one. Third, Ecclesiastes, the book that lists the seasons of a life, gives "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." In that line, silence comes first. Fourth, why this works, even outside scripture. Advice, even good advice, can quietly tell a hurting person they're a problem to be solved. Presence tells them they're a person worth staying with. Some chaplains and counselors use a simple question before offering anything: do you want ideas, or do you want me to listen? Then they take the answer seriously. Sometimes the answer is ideas, and then advice is a gift. But asked first, it lands as care instead of correction.
screen: `MISERABLE COMFORTERS ARE YE ALL.` · `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · `A TIME TO KEEP SILENCE.` · `IDEAS, OR LISTENING?` · then, large: `LESS ADVICE.`

segments.voice: This is a rehearsal for later. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone who's having a hard time. In your mind, sit down beside them. They start to talk. Notice whether an urge to fix rises: in the chest, on the tongue, a ready answer. Let it rise, and let it pass, like a car going by. Instead, say only: that sounds hard; tell me more. Then just listen, and stay with them in the quiet until the bell. If you pray, you can hold them there too. The bell holds the time.
Less advice. Presence before solutions: swift to hear, slow to speak, and a time to keep silence. Today's word.
Your line: less advice. Today, when someone tells you about a problem, ask one question before offering a single fix: do you want ideas, or do you want me to listen? Day seven hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Hospital and hospice chaplains of different traditions are trained in listening, and some Christians recall James 1:19, swift to hear, slow to speak, when they sit with those who are struggling.
